subtitle: Six Years That Remade the Century
controlling_argument: World War II was so total in its violence that it ended the era of great-power war on this scale - and the peace built in 1945 is the world order we still live inside.

slides.job_to_be_done: Awe at the scale and finality of the war, before a single fact lands
slides.title: THE LAST WORLD WAR
slides.subtitle: Six Years That Remade the Century
slides.tagline: SIX YEARS  ·  SIXTY MILLION LIVES  ·  ONE NEW WORLD ORDER
slides.sub_tagline: At least 60 million dead, a majority of them civilians - and a peace agreement that still governs the planet
slides.credit: Photograph: US Marines raise the flag on Iwo Jima, Feb 1945 (Joe Rosenthal, US Gov / public domain)

speaker_notes.transition: Open with the frame and the claim - this is one of the only photographs almost everyone can name, and it was taken on a volcanic island 7,000 miles from Berlin. That spread is the point.
speaker_notes.elaboration: Every conflict before this one had been, at most, regional. World War II was fought on the ground in Europe, Africa, and Asia, across every ocean, and from the Arctic to the Solomon Islands. The real number underneath all the dates is the death count: the current consensus estimate is sixty to seventy-five million, and for the first time in any war most of them were civilians. That is roughly three percent of every person alive in 1940 - ended in six years.
speaker_notes.bridge: So before we talk about armies and battles, let's sit with the scale of the event itself - because every slide after this is measured against it.

slides.job_to_be_done: Make the audience feel the war's shape in two figures: six years and a death toll
slides.title: The Deadliest Conflict in History
slides.insight_bar: No event in recorded history killed a larger share of humanity - about one person in thirty, worldwide

speaker_notes.transition: You've seen the photograph; now the two numbers that should genuinely change how you think about this war.
speaker_notes.elaboration: Six years sounds short - shorter than the career of a professional footballer. But measure the density. In barely two thousand days the war killed sixty to seventy-five million people. For scale: every soldier, sailor, airman and civilian - the war took about one in thirty of the whole human species as it stood in 1940. The physical damage matched the human: Berlin, Warsaw, London, Rotterdam, Tokyo, Manila, and hundreds of others were reduced to rubble fields that took two decades to clear.
speaker_notes.bridge: A war this destructive does not begin at full size - it escalates from smaller crises. Let's trace the road in.

slides.job_to_be_done: Show that WW2 was a decade of escalating crises that became global, not one sudden war
slides.title: It Did Not Start Global

nodes.title: Manchuria
nodes.body: Japan invades; the League of Nations protests and does nothing. First alarm.

nodes.title: Full Invasion
nodes.body: Japan's war on China begins in earnest; millions die before 1939.

nodes.title: Poland, 1 Sept
nodes.body: Germany invades; Britain and France declare war two days later.

nodes.title: Global by Default
nodes.body: Barbarossa in June; Pearl Harbor in December. Now it is a world war.

speaker_notes.transition: Every coalition war has a fuse that runs back further than the official start date. This one was really lit in Asia eight years before Europe's war began.
speaker_notes.elaboration: In 1931 Japan took Manchuria and the League of Nations sent a report it could not enforce. In 1937 Japan's full invasion of China turned into a conflict that would eventually kill somewhere between fifteen and twenty million Chinese - many people do not realise the war in Asia was already staggering by 1939. In Europe, Germany remilitarised the Rhineland, annexed Austria, took Czechoslovakia, and still Britain and France adjusted their strategy rather than fight. Then came the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact of 1939, which let Hitler invade Poland without a second front.
speaker_notes.bridge: The point of the timeline is not the dates - it's that each failure to stop small aggression made the next one bigger. That escalation produced the two coalitions we'll look at now.

slides.job_to_be_done: Make the audience feel the asymmetry between a loose opportunistic pact and a global alliance
slides.title: Two Coalitions, One War

bullets: Britain, the USSR, the US, and China
peak 1942, from the Atlantic to the Pacific
declared war on the US after Pearl Harbor

speaker_notes.transition: The timelines explain how the war grew; the coalitions explain how it was won and nearly lost.
speaker_notes.elaboration: The Axis was an alliance of convenience, not of ideology - Japan and Germany had even been geopolitically hostile through the 1930s. Its three founders never agreed a shared strategy: Germany worked for a European empire, Japan for an Asian one, Italy for a Mediterranean revival. The Allies were just as strange in their own way - communist Russia, capitalist America, imperial Britain and republican China were enemies of each other's systems, united only by a common foe. Their stated goal from Casablanca in 1943 was unconditional surrender, which meant the Axis would not be allowed to negotiate its way out.
speaker_notes.bridge: Inside those coalitions, the war was fought as 'total war' - every factory, lab, and citizen mobilised. That machinery is the next thing to understand.

slides.job_to_be_done: Explain that this was the first war won by whole economies, not only armies
slides.title: The Whole Society Mobilized

pillars.title: Industry
pillars.stat: ~296,000 aircraft built in the US alone

pillars.title: Home Front
bullets: farms fed armies before their towns

pillars.title: Science
pillars.stat: radar, penicillin, jets, the atomic bomb

speaker_notes.transition: Total war means the distinction between soldier and civilian disappears - and that is visible in how every belligerent rebuilt itself overnight.
speaker_notes.elaboration: Consider just one country. American shipyards took roughly four years and a hundred days each to produce over twenty-seven hundred Liberty ships; Ford's plant at Willow Run turned out a B-24 bomber every hour at peak. On the other side, when German panzers pushed toward Moscow in 1941, the Soviets dismantled about fifteen hundred factories and relocated them east of the Ural mountains, some producing within a hundred days of arriving. And notice the label says home front, not home - in Britain, food, clothing and fuel were rationed from 1940 until 1954, nearly a decade after the war ended.
speaker_notes.bridge: These economies did not just supply battles - they decided which side could afford to keep losing and absorb the cost. Let's name the real ledger.

speaker_notes.transition: The alliances and the factories give the shape; these four numbers give the weight.
speaker_notes.elaboration: Take the top row seriously, because our brains are built to underweight large numbers. Sixty to seventy-five million people - and more than half of them were civilians. A hundred million soldiers were mobilized, which in a world of 2.3 billion people meant one in roughly twenty of everyone alive was under arms. When you read that about three percent of the entire species died inside that one conflict, set it against the First World War, where the comparable figure was closer to one percent. And it was genuinely global - over fifty independent states were formally at war.
speaker_notes.bridge: Every one of those numbers is a person, and the next slide stops counting altogether - it just lets someone speak.

slides.job_to_be_done: Emotional pause - let one documented voice carry the cost before the data peak
slides.title: So Much Owed to So Few
slides.quote: Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.
slides.attribution: — Winston Churchill, House of Commons, 20 August 1940
takeaways: roughly 3,000 RAF pilots, average age about 20
outnumbered by German bombers and fighters that summer
the planned invasion of Britain was postponed indefinitely

speaker_notes.transition: We have been on the scale of millions. It matters to come down to the scale of a few thousand people making a decision on a Tuesday.
speaker_notes.elaboration: Churchill was praising the Royal Air Force pilots of the summer of 1940 - roughly three thousand of them, many still in their early twenties, flying fighters like the Spitfire and Hurricane against a German air force of several thousand aircraft that was trying to break Britain before any invasion could land. They were chronically short of pilots, and the average pilot who survived was promoted twice in a month because the ranks kept emptying. The invasion barges Hitler had gathered were stood down once the air force gave him no chance.
speaker_notes.bridge: Churchill called it the Few - but the heaviest price of the war was not paid by them. It was paid by the civilians of two continents, which is what the ledger next shows.

slides.job_to_be_done: Prove with data that the war's center of gravity was the East and the civilian sphere, overturning Western-leaning intuitions
slides.title: Counting the Uncountable

callout.label: TOTAL
callout.insight: Civilian deaths outnumbered military ones - for the first time in any war. Soviet and Chinese losses dwarfed the West's.

speaker_notes.transition: Here is the ledger the previous slide promised - and it corrects a common Western assumption about where the war was actually fought.
speaker_notes.elaboration: Everything in this table is a rounded estimate, because counting the dead of a world war is an act of demography performed in ruins - figures for China alone range from fifteen to twenty-five million. But the shape is clear. The Soviet Union carried the heaviest single burden, roughly twenty-seven million dead. China lost maybe as many as twenty million. Notice the American column: four hundred thousand - tragic, but a rounding error against the Eastern Front. And the civilian column overturns the old arithmetic: more people died out of uniform than in it. Poland lost nearly a fifth of its population, including six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust.
speaker_notes.bridge: This is the number-shaped reason the war's survivors built the postwar world the way they did. Which is exactly our last act.

slides.job_to_be_done: Locate the decisive reversals in 1942-43 and the cascade that made Allied victory structurally certain
slides.title: The Tide Turned Twice
bullets: four Japanese carriers sunk; the Pacific initiative over
the 6th Army surrendered; Germany's first great defeat
the largest tank battle halted the last eastern offensive
156,000 troops landed on five beaches in one day
Hitler dead, the Wehrmacht surrendered, Europe fell silent

stat_card.headline: Putting It on the Axis
stat_card.subtitle: Midway · Stalingrad · Kursk · D-Day - losses no coalition could replace

speaker_notes.transition: We have the cost and the coalitions. Now, where exactly did the war turn, and why does the answer sit in one disputed year?
speaker_notes.elaboration: The turning points cluster in 1942-43 because the Axis overextended on its two widest fronts at once. In the Pacific, Midway in June 1942 cost Japan four fleet carriers in a single afternoon; with them went the ability to replace trained aircrews, and after that the Pacific was a slow, grinding retreat. On the Eastern Front, the German 6th Army was surrounded at Stalingrad and surrendered in February 1943 - the largest surrender in German military history. Kursk confirmed it four months later in the biggest tank battle ever fought. The Axis fact is now acts as a declining graph: once the Allies' factories and manpower began to outrun the Axis in 1943, no tactical genius could reverse it - only slow the timetable.
speaker_notes.bridge: So the war was decided roughly four years in - and the last slide asked what was built from the wreckage, which is the peace we still live in.

slides.job_to_be_done: Synthesise the war's five legacies and complicate the easy 'good war' story
slides.title: The Peace We Still Live In

cards.label: A New Architecture
cards.body: The UN Charter was signed in 1945 and the Nuremberg trials made crimes against humanity a legal, not moral, fact.
cards.body2: The great powers promised to talk first and fight last.

cards.label: Empires Ended
cards.body: The war bankrupted and discredited the colonial powers; within a generation most of Africa and Asia had independent states.
cards.body2: A map already redrawn once was redrawn again in the Cold War.

banner.label: THE ECHO
banner.big: The nuclear age, the Cold War, and the United Nations were all born inside these six years.
banner.closer: So far - at that scale - no war has repeated the last one.

speaker_notes.transition: Wars end in treaties; this one ended in an architecture. Almost everything you'd list as 'modern world' descends from 1945.
speaker_notes.elaboration: The UN replaced the failed League in 1945 with 51 members and the veto-holding Security Council. The Nuremberg trials of 1945-46 established that individuals, not just states, could be tried for crimes against humanity - a legal first. The war also ended empires: Britain and France emerged triumphant but bankrupt, and by the 1960s most of Africa and Asia were independent. But the honest complication belongs here too: the victory powers had no clean hands - Allied firebombing of Dresden and Tokyo, the atomic bombs, and Soviet brutality in the occupied East all mean 'the good war' is a partial label. And the peace inherited the war's tension.
speaker_notes.bridge: That tension became the Cold War - fifty years of nuclear standoff that inherited the colossal weaponry of 1945. And yet.

slides.job_to_be_done: Resolve the argument on an echo of the title: the scale has not been repeated, and the peace is why
slides.title: THE LAST WORLD WAR
slides.closing_line: The peace that followed is the world we still share.
slides.credit: Photograph: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin at Yalta, February 1945 (US Gov / public domain)

speaker_notes.transition: We opened with the photograph of Iwo Jima and the claim that this was the last world war. Close by honoring that claim exactly.
speaker_notes.elaboration: It has been over eighty years since September 1939, and no conflict has come close to the scale of 1939-45 - no sixty million dead, no hundred million mobilized, no coalition of fifty states against a pact of three. That is not because humanity became kinder at war. It is because the survivors built institutions - the UN, the veto, the nuclear taboo - designed to make great-power war unaffordable, and because the bomb made any repeat of the six-year war unspeakable in a new way. The Yalta photograph is the hinge of it all: the Big Three dividing the map of what would become the Cold War.
speaker_notes.bridge: The photograph behind me is not from the war's end as celebration, but from its negotiation. The last world war was built in six years - and it has taken every year since to build the peace. So far, it holds.
